name: 24LC512T-I_SN
title: 24AA512, 24LC512, 24FC512: 512 Kbit (64K x 8) I2C serial EEPROM
summary: A 512 Kbit EEPROM organised as 65,536 bytes, reached over a two-wire I2C-compatible bus. Three grades are covered: 24AA512 runs from 1.7 V at up to 400 kHz, 24LC512 from 2.5 V at 400 kHz, and 24FC512 from 1.7 V at up to 1 MHz. Writes go through a 128-byte page buffer and are self-timed, 5 ms at most; three address pins let eight parts share one bus, and a WP pin locks the whole array. 24LC512T-I/SN is the 2.5 V grade, industrial temperature, in an 8-lead 3.90 mm SOIC on tape and reel.

rows: 8-ball chip scale (CS), tape and reel only
notes: The order code is device, optional T for tape and reel, a dash, the temperature letter (I or E), a slash and the package code: 24LC512T-I/SN is a 24LC512 on tape and reel, industrial range, 8-lead SOIC. X stands for the temperature letter.
Temperature letters: I = -40 °C to +85 °C, E = -40 °C to +125 °C. Only 24LC512 comes in E.
The chip scale package comes only as 24AA512, industrial range, on tape and reel. The 17K in its code marks the 160K process technology.
24FC512 is the high-speed grade.

equations.expr: page start = k × 128, page end = k × 128 + 127
equations.note: A page write stays inside one such page.

equations.name: Extended address across cascaded parts
equations.expr: A16 = A0 bit, A17 = A1 bit, A18 = A2 bit of the control byte

where.A16..A18: upper bits of a 4 Mbit space formed by up to eight parts on one bus

equations.note: A sequential read does not carry over from one part to the next.

operation.text: A0, A1 and A2 give each part a three-bit address; the part answers only when control-byte bits A2 A1 A0 equal the levels on these pins, so up to eight parts can share a bus. The pins are tied to VCC or VSS. Where a microcontroller or logic drives them instead, they must sit at a valid 0 or 1 before the part is used.

SDA carries addresses and data both ways and is an open-drain output, so the bus needs a pull-up to VCC: typically 10 kΩ at 100 kHz and 2 kΩ at 400 kHz and 1 MHz. SDA may change only while SCL is low; a change while SCL is high signals Start or Stop.

WP is tied to VSS or VCC. At VSS writes are allowed. At VCC the entire array (0000-FFFF) is protected: write commands are acknowledged but nothing is written, the part is ready for a new command at once, and reads carry on normally. WP is read at the Stop of each write command; changing it after that Stop does not affect the write cycle already started.
The part is a slave on a two-wire bus. A master drives SCL, controls bus access and creates Start and Stop. Either side can transmit or receive; the master decides which.

Bus idle: SDA and SCL both high. Start: SDA falls while SCL is high; every command begins with one. Stop: SDA rises while SCL is high; every operation ends with one. Data valid: after a Start, SDA held steady through the high half of SCL is one data bit, and data changes in the low half. A transfer may begin only on an idle bus; the master sets how many bytes pass between Start and Stop.

Each byte is followed by a ninth clock from the master, during which the addressed receiver pulls SDA low and keeps it low for the whole high phase, with setup and hold times met. While an internal write is in progress the part acknowledges nothing. At the end of a read the master leaves the last byte unacknowledged; the part then releases SDA high so the master can send Stop.

The first byte after Start is the control byte: control code 1010, chip select bits A2 A1 A0, then R/W (1 read, 0 write). On a matching code and select bits the part acknowledges and enters read or write. Two address bytes follow for a write or random read, high byte first; all of A15 to A0 are used. The chip select bits act as the three most significant address bits, so software can treat A0, A1, A2 of the control byte as A16, A17, A18 across eight parts (4 Mbit); a sequential read cannot run across from one part to the next.

The master sends Start, a control byte carrying R/W = 0, the address high byte, the address low byte and one data byte, the part acknowledging each, then Stop. The Stop starts the self-timed internal write cycle (TWC, 5 ms max) during which the part does not acknowledge. Afterwards the address counter points at the location after the one written.

As for a byte write, but the master keeps sending data, up to 127 more bytes after the first, before Stop. Bytes are held in the 128-byte on-chip buffer and committed to memory as one cycle after Stop. After each byte the lower seven address bits count up by one; sending more than 128 bytes before Stop wraps the counter and overwrites the earliest bytes received.

Physical pages are 128 bytes long and begin at whole multiples of 128. A page write never crosses into the next page: bytes beyond the end wrap to the start of the current page and overwrite what is there. Application software has to keep page writes inside one page.
A write of fewer than 128 bytes still refreshes the rest of its page along with the new bytes, so the whole page goes through a write cycle. Endurance is therefore rated per page.

Because the part ignores the bus while writing, the master can find the end of a write cycle by polling: right after the Stop that starts the write, send Start and a control byte carrying R/W = 0. No acknowledge means the cycle is still running, so repeat the Start and control byte. An acknowledge means the cycle is over and the following command can be sent at once.

The internal address counter holds the last address accessed plus one. Sending a control byte carrying R/W = 1 makes the part acknowledge and return the byte at that address (n + 1 after an access to n). The master does not acknowledge it and sends Stop.

To read any address, the master first starts a write (R/W = 0) and sends the two address bytes, which loads the address counter. It then issues a new Start without a Stop, sends a control byte carrying R/W = 1, receives one byte, does not acknowledge, and sends Stop. The counter then points to the next address.

Begun like a current address or random read, but the master acknowledges each byte it receives and the part sends the next address in turn. The master ends by leaving the final byte unacknowledged and sending Stop. The counter rolls over from FFFF to 0000, so the whole memory can be read in one operation.
Inputs have Schmitt triggers to reject noise, and the output edge rate is controlled to avoid ground bounce.
